chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
title: The Crawley date with Jelly Roll Morton and Russell, retold
summary: Morton and Russell both arrived to back Crawley, split the numbers, and traded barbs about the Lafayette versus the Paramount; Holmes recalls Morton's hard times.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: What do you remember of the recordings?
Well...
Because some of them had Jelly Roll Morton on them.

I don't know that the recording... They was his recordings. But something happened. He had Russell's group to come in, to record with him. And while we were there, Jelly Roll Morton walks in with a group, and he's supposed to record with him.. I don't know how they got mixed up. The two of them... Jelly had his group there to record with Wilton Crawley, and so did Russell.

So anyway, he was (?) out there (?) with so-and-so, and we split up the band or something like that. We both do the recording. So Jelly would play a little piano on some of the numbers and Russell would play the piano on some of the
numbers. I would play the saxophone on some of the numbers, and then somebody else would play. It was agreeable. And nothing was nerve-wracking or anything.
Did Russell and Jelly ever play together on the recording?
No.
So that you had four hands?
Not that I know of, no. Could have, but I don't know. Because I wasn't paying that much attention to them. Because when I wasn't on, I was doing something else around the studio.
But you remember that there were separate sessions. Some of them were months apart.

Oh yeah. Well, they were different, yeah. Well, that happened... Well, I mean, all of them wasn't like that. I mean, Russell would go in with his group, the next group. Well, I don't know if Jelly was making the records for him, too, any more. But I was just telling you about that particular time when the two bands got together there.
I remember you said they were like two prima donnas squaring off.
Oh yeah. Well, see, that sort of caused some dissension, you know. Because Jelly thought he was going to be the star, and Wilton Crawley knew he was the

star. He knew it was his show. And Jelly thought Mister Jelly Lord was gonna take over, and he'd come in and: "Hi, Wilton. Caught your show last week at the Lafayette Theatre." So Wilton said, "Yeah?" He said, "Well, next week, I'm at the Paramount." The Paramount is downtown. The Lafayette Theatre is a little colored theatre up inn Harlem. See, Jelly Roll was very sarcastic about it. But Wilton, he come right back at him: "Next week I'm at the Paramount."
Of course, at the time Jelly was not...

At the time Jelly wasn't doing good. Jelly would have been glad to be anywhere. At that time he would have been glad to be in the Lafayette. He wasn't doing good. Jelly did not do good. See, Jelly didn't take New York by storm. I didn't know Jelly was a big man in the music business until years later. I had to read it in a book, Jelly Roll Morton was the big man from New Orleans. I said, "That must be a different Jelly Roll than the one I know." Because Jelly Roll, he was going through some hard times around here in New York, just like King Oliver was. But King Oliver had an excuse. His gums was bad. You know, he had pyorrhea; he couldn't blow.
But Jelly could talk. Oh, and he could talk and he would talk. He'd talk the leg off an iron pot. And he was

very educational! I mean, to listen to. He said some mighty witty things, you know. He was the type of guy, you'd hate him if you first hear him. But then, the more you listen to him, the better you would like him, you know. You'd stop paying attention to some of the things that he was saying, and you had to like him for it.

That session... They turned out all right. All of them sessions turned out all right. There was just so many musicians around there, it was hard to tell who was playing on what. But everything turned out nice. Yup, a lot of musicians in the studio that day. I mean, you wouldn't overwork yourself. You know, you'd be playing on this number, and when you finished that number, somebody else would take you up and they'd play another number. So you didn't work too hard. Very good.
